doc.title: Vince Lateano interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Recording with Tania Maria for Concord
summary: He recounts the unrehearsed session at Coast Recorders with Tania Maria and what happened to her.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: I have one more piece of music that you’re on here. See if you recognize—
Yeah. Tania, Tania Maria. Is this “Yatra-ta?” © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

Okay. This, interesting story. I’m with Cal Tjader, right? Probably ’80 or thereabouts, ’81. And Carl Jefferson, who is Concord Records, calls and said, “I want you to do this, we’re going to do a record with a Brazilian piano player singer that I just signed and no one ever knew about it.” And I said, “Okay.” So he hired Cal’s — me, Cal’s drummer and bass player, Rob Fisher. And — is Poncho on that? Is Poncho on that do you know? I don’t have the liner note with me. It’s either Poncho or a local conga player named Willie, a conga drummer named Willie Colon.

Willie Colon. Okay, not Willie Colon the New York trombone player. Yeah I don’t think Poncho did this. Anyway so we show up at the Coast Recorders and Tania is there and we meet her and she speaks very little English. And no rehearsal or anything we’re just in the studio and getting ready to do this thing. And so nothing is written out. And she says, I mean well let’s hear what you’re going to do. So she launches into this tune, this first tune, and we all looked at each other like what are we gonna do my God? I mean this whole thing that she had worked out. And we just worked it out and recorded it. And that’s how it came out. But the panic look on everybody’s face, we’re in the studio and we’re going to make this record, and that was it. After a few mis-runs or whatever you want to call them, we came up with that. And got through it somehow, and the rest of the record — oh Eddie Duran’s on that, the guitarist, he’s on there. And but that was the first thing we did and of course I think that was the hardest thing, which is good, get that out of the way. But it was like oh my God I’m in deep do-do now. But she is great. I mean boy. You’re talking about —
What happened to her is she still around?

She was, let’s see, when I met her she was living in Paris I think. And she’s from Brazil. And she lived in Paris. And then she moved here shortly after and lived in I guess lived in New York for many years, for quite a few years. And now I understand she’s back in Europe. I’m not sure where. But I mean I sort of kept track, when she would come through town, she got more into like a Latin funk thing, pop Latin funk. And she could do that. She was really something. I mean I was awed by her. She’s got a lot of talent you know. But that what we did there was probably the jazziest thing she ever — I mean with acoustic instruments, you know what I mean, that kind of thing. But that was, boy you talk about the look on our faces when she launched into that it was oh my God.
That’s cool. Desperation leads to inspiration.

Well I guess. But the thing is, it’s one thing to be at a rehearsal and be in trouble. But to be at a recording studio, and because the clock is ticking, it’s like you feel this pressure. But it really came out pretty good I thought in retrospect. It’s like wow. © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-
